extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, epistemologists, historians of science, and advanced graduate students or researchers interested in the conceptual foundations of scientific progress and evolutionary analogies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying conceptual criteria for evaluating the growth of scientific knowledge, the significance of lines of inquiry, and the analogy between epistemic success and evolutionary success (including branching/lineage addition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical trends as constraints on theories of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Any historical trend exhibited by knowledge is prima facie epistemologically significant: the formulation, development, and refinement of a theory involves responding to the factors that function as constraints on a theory in the relevant domain; viable theories obey the constraints recognized by a research community at a given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical patterns (e.g., long-term growth of knowledge) as empirical phenomena that a credible theory of knowledge should accommodate. The text emphasizes that histories provide phenomena to which theories about knowledge may legitimately be asked to apply (cf. Kuhn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth as an index of epistemic success (causal connection to successful outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical growth of knowledge is epistemologically significant because growth is often treated as an index of success; success typically demands a causal explanation rather than attribution to brute luck, so growth provides prima facie evidence that knowledge causally contributes to successful outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed epistemic advantages or successes are plausibly causally connected to the accumulation of knowledge, and consider counterfactual scenarios (e.g., static knowledge) to test the robustness of causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical progress (refinement-oriented success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertical progress: movement toward an optimum in practice space, characterized by refinement of practice and improved solutions to problems. This form of success is compatible with zero or even negative growth in the number of lines of inquiry (contraction or stasis) because it concerns deepening mastery rather than proliferation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging progress of a practice or theory, distinguish refinement of methods or understanding (vertical) from mere increase in the number of topics investigated; refinement may reduce the scope of inquiry while improving explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal progress (growth-centered success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizontal progress: the broadening of understanding via the addition of new (refinable) lines of inquiry; measured as a positive trend in the number of phenomena of which we have at least a dim understanding. Horizontal progress is largely content-independent: it counts the addition of lines regardless of later reconceptualizations of their content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an addition to scientific practice constitutes a new refineable line of inquiry that broadens the set of problems being investigated; count durable additions as horizontal progress even if their internal content later changes drastically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of a line of inquiry (community-judged lasting contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Def: a line of inquiry is significant just in case it is judged by a community of practitioners to make a lasting contribution to human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lines of inquiry by community judgment and by their persistence: ephemeral or short-lived investigations do not qualify as significant. Emphasize communal assessment and durability as central tests of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lineage (or line-of-inquiry) addition counts only if persistent
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a lineage (biological) or a line of inquiry (epistemic) counts as growth only if its effects persist for an appreciable duration on macroevolutionary or historical timescales; ephemeral branches do not constitute meaningful growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring growth, discount transient offshoots that quickly go extinct or are abandoned; require appreciable longevity before treating an addition as contributing to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Individual longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual longevity: how long an individual organism lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evolutionary contexts this is one way to conceive of 'success' at the level of single organisms; in epistemic analogy, consider temporality of contributions at the individual-agent level, but note the text primarily uses this to populate the taxonomy of evolutionary success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Species longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Species longevity: for a higher-level taxon, the average duration of time between when a species first appears in the fossil record and when it disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a measure of evolutionary stability over time; analogously, assess how long an entire research program or paradigm persists as an indicator of epistemic robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Species fecundity
rubrics_metrics.description: Species fecundity: the number of daughter species produced by a given species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a metric of evolutionary diversification; in epistemic terms, count how many new subfields or distinct research lines a program spawns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Individual abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual abundance: the number of organisms that are members of a given lineage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat abundance as a proxy for local stability and resilience; epistemically, consider the number of practitioners or amount of activity devoted to a line as indicating its robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Percentage of the planet’s biomass
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of the planet’s biomass: the proportion of the organic material comprising a lineage, relative to the total amount of organic material on Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coarse large-scale metric of dominance; analogy in science might be the proportionate cognitive/organizational resources devoted to a domain, though the text notes this is one variant among many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Species that co-opt other species
rubrics_metrics.description: Species that co-opt other species for their betterment: species that either manipulate or exterminate other species, resulting in an increase in individual abundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures success via ecological interactions that boost a lineage; epistemically, consider whether a research line accumulates advantages by appropriating methods, tools, or topics from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Wide geographic range
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide geographic range: a lineage for which the members that are farthest apart from one another are far apart in an absolute sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range indicates exposure to varied environments and hence different selective challenges; in epistemic analogy, evaluate how widely a line of inquiry applies across domains or contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward's metric: Surviving mass extinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Surviving mass extinctions: lineages that were not driven to extinction during at least one of the major extinction events in the history of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high bar for stability across radical environmental change; analogically, ask whether a research program endures through major paradigm shifts or social upheavals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary success as relative growth in problem-solving capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A generalized conception: evolutionary success involves a clade’s relative growth along any dimension associated with stability across environmental change; at any given level, success is distinguished by relative growth in problem-solving capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a unifying criterion: measure growth in terms of increased capacity to solve qualitatively different or more numerous problems (abundance, diversity, geographic range, etc.). This connects evolutionary metrics to epistemic growth via the notion of added problem-solving capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of success-metrics (nested environmental challenges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of evolutionary success fit a nested hierarchy of environmental challenges: abundance relates to local/population problems, species diversity/longevity to lineage-level problems, geographic range to broader environmental diversity, and surviving mass extinctions to the broadest set of challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating success, recognize the hierarchical relation: success at one level implies competence at a corresponding scale of environmental challenge. Apply analogous hierarchical thinking to levels of epistemic practice (individuals, research programs, disciplines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-independence of horizontal progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizontal progress is concerned with the cardinality of phenomena under investigation and generally does not require that our views about its constituents remain fixed; once a line of inquiry is added, horizontal progress is achieved even if earlier beliefs about that line are abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate addition of new lines (breadth) with correctness of their initial content; count durable expansion of inquiry-areas as progress regardless of later reconceptualizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that epistemic significance correlate with selection-like processes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the perpetual emergence of significant lines of inquiry is epistemically important, and if epistemic importance is explained by natural selection’s causal responsibility, then a line of inquiry's probability of significance should increase directly with natural selection’s influence on the modification of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that scientific communities exhibit selection-like mechanisms (e.g., differential retention, variation and selection of practices); evaluate whether such mechanisms plausibly increase the likelihood that new lines become significant (lasting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability/stability across contexts as an epistemic desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth that is historically stable across varied sociocultural, intellectual, and environmental conditions is especially epistemically significant, because such stability suggests insensitivity to perturbations and persistence across contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer accounts of progress or success that show robustness across changes in context; when testing claims of epistemic growth, examine whether the phenomenon persists across diverse conditions rather than being contingent on narrow circumstances.
